definition.text: Classical conditioning is a process by which we learn to associate stimuli and, consequently, to anticipate events — a neutral stimulus repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus comes to trigger a learned response on its own.

anchor.quote: a process by which we learn to associate stimuli and, consequently, to anticipate events

facts.text: An unconditioned stimulus (UCS) elicits a reflexive response in an organism with no learning required.

anchor.quote: an unconditioned stimulus (UCS): a stimulus that elicits a reflexive response in an organism

facts.text: An unconditioned response (UCR) is a natural, unlearned reaction to a given stimulus — Pavlov's dogs salivating to meat powder.

anchor.quote: an unconditioned response (UCR): a natural (unlearned) reaction to a given stimulus

facts.text: A conditioned stimulus (CS) is a stimulus that elicits a response only after repeatedly being paired with an unconditioned stimulus.

anchor.quote: the conditioned stimulus (CS), which is a stimulus that elicits a response after repeatedly being paired with an unconditioned stimulus

facts.text: Extinction is the decrease in the conditioned response when the unconditioned stimulus stops accompanying the conditioned stimulus.

anchor.quote: Extinction is the decrease in the conditioned response when the unconditioned stimulus is no longer presented with the conditioned stimulus

facts.text: Spontaneous recovery is the return of a previously extinguished conditioned response following a rest period.

anchor.quote: the return of a previously extinguished conditioned response following a rest period

misconceptions.text: Students label any stimulus that triggers behavior a conditioned stimulus, blurring the UCS/CS distinction.
misconceptions.corrective: An unconditioned stimulus elicits a reflex with no learning at all; a stimulus is conditioned only after repeated pairing with the UCS turns a formerly neutral stimulus into a trigger.

examples.text: The smell of a dentist's office (CS) making a patient's heart race after past pairings with the drill (UCS) — anticipation learned, not chosen.

definition.text: In operant conditioning, organisms learn to associate a behavior and its consequence: reinforced behaviors become more likely, punished behaviors less likely.

anchor.quote: organisms learn to associate a behavior and its consequence

facts.text: The law of effect: behaviors followed by satisfying consequences are more likely to be repeated; behaviors followed by unpleasant consequences are less likely.

anchor.quote: behaviors that are followed by consequences that are satisfying to the organism are more likely to be repeated

facts.text: In operant terms, positive means adding something and negative means taking something away — not good and bad.

anchor.quote: positive means you are adding something, and negative means you are taking something away

facts.text: Reinforcement always increases a behavior and punishment always decreases it, whichever sign it carries.

anchor.quote: Reinforcement means you are increasing a behavior, and punishment means you are decreasing a behavior

facts.text: In negative reinforcement, an undesirable stimulus is removed to increase a behavior.

anchor.quote: In negative reinforcement, an undesirable stimulus is removed to increase a behavior

facts.text: Shaping builds complex behavior by rewarding successive approximations of a target behavior.

anchor.quote: we reward successive approximations of a target behavior

misconceptions.text: Students equate negative reinforcement with punishment.
misconceptions.corrective: Negative refers to removing a stimulus, not to badness: negative reinforcement removes something undesirable to increase a behavior, while punishment of either sign decreases behavior.

misconceptions.text: Students read positive and negative as good and bad outcomes.
misconceptions.corrective: In operant conditioning positive means adding something and negative means taking something away; either operation can serve reinforcement or punishment.

examples.text: A teacher excuses students from Friday homework when the class stays on task all week — removing an undesirable task to increase on-task behavior (negative reinforcement).

definition.text: In observational learning, we learn by watching others and then imitating, or modeling, what they do or say — no direct reinforcement of the learner is required.

anchor.quote: we learn by watching others and then imitating, or modeling, what they do or say

facts.text: Bandura researched modeling behavior, particularly children's modeling of adults' aggressive and violent behaviors.

anchor.quote: Bandura researched modeling behavior, particularly children's modeling of adults' aggressive and violent behaviors

facts.text: Successful modeling requires four steps in order: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation.

anchor.quote: steps in the process of modeling that must be followed if learning is to be successful: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation

facts.text: Seeing a model reinforced makes the observer more motivated to copy them — vicarious reinforcement.

anchor.quote: If you saw that the model was reinforced for their behavior, you will be more motivated to copy them

facts.text: Seeing a model punished makes the observer less motivated to copy them — vicarious punishment; children who saw the model punished decreased their imitation.

anchor.quote: If you observed the model being punished, you would be less motivated to copy them

facts.text: Observational learning can have both prosocial and antisocial effects, so the models children see matter.

anchor.quote: this learning can have both prosocial and antisocial effects

misconceptions.text: Students assume a person must be directly rewarded themselves before imitation occurs.
misconceptions.corrective: Bandura showed vicarious consequences suffice: children imitated a model who was praised or simply not punished, and held back when the model was punished — the consequence landed on the model, not the child.

examples.text: A new student watches a classmate get praised for raising a hand before speaking and starts raising their own hand — vicarious reinforcement in action.

definition.text: Memory is the set of processes used to encode, store, and retrieve information over different periods of time; to be stored long term, information must pass through sensory, short-term, and long-term stages.

anchor.quote: Memory is the set of processes used to encode, store, and retrieve information over different periods of time

facts.text: Encoding is the input of information into the memory system.

anchor.quote: the input of information into the memory system

facts.text: Words encoded semantically — by their meaning — are remembered better than words encoded visually or acoustically.

anchor.quote: Words that had been encoded semantically were better remembered than those encoded visually or acoustically

facts.text: Storage is the creation of a permanent record of information.

anchor.quote: Storage is the creation of a permanent record of information

facts.text: A memory headed for long-term storage must pass through three distinct stages: sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory.

anchor.quote: it has to pass through three distinct stages: Sensory Memory, Short-Term Memory, and finally Long-Term Memory

facts.text: Retrieval is the act of getting information out of memory storage and back into conscious awareness.

anchor.quote: The act of getting information out of memory storage and back into conscious awareness is known as retrieval

misconceptions.text: Students picture memory as one big storehouse where information simply sits once seen.
misconceptions.corrective: Memory is a set of processes, not a place: information must be encoded, pass through sensory and short-term stages into long-term storage, and then be retrieved — and it can be lost at every step.

examples.text: Explaining a new term in your own words (semantic encoding) beats recopying it ten times — meaning-based processing is the deepest route into storage.

long-term memory, then short-term memory, then sensory memory
sensory memory, then long-term memory, then short-term memory

mapping.stages: encoding into sensory memory, holding in short-term memory, consolidating into long-term memory
mapping.dependency: each stage hands its product to the next — unencoded input cannot be rehearsed, unrehearsed traces never reach long-term storage
mapping.failure if skipped: information is lost and there is nothing left to retrieve

definition.text: Short-term memory (STM) is a temporary storage system that processes incoming sensory memory; the related term working memory emphasizes active manipulation, and the two terms are not exactly the same.

anchor.quote: Short-term memory (STM) is a temporary storage system that processes incoming sensory memory

facts.text: Short-term memory storage lasts only about 15 to 30 seconds without rehearsal.

anchor.quote: Short-term memory storage lasts 15 to 30 seconds

facts.text: For most people short-term capacity is close to 7 plus or minus 2 items.

anchor.quote: the capacity will probably be close to 7 plus or minus 2

facts.text: Active rehearsal is a way of attending to information to move it from short-term to long-term memory.

anchor.quote: Active rehearsal is a way of attending to information to move it from short-term to long-term memory

facts.text: Short-term memory and working memory are sometimes used interchangeably, but they are not exactly the same.

anchor.quote: The terms short-term and working memory are sometimes used interchangeably, but they are not exactly the same

facts.text: Sensory memory holds brief sensory events such as sights and sounds for only up to a couple of seconds before they fade or move on.

anchor.quote: storage of brief sensory events, such as sights, sounds, and tastes

misconceptions.text: Students believe short-term memory holds information for hours, like a mental notepad left open all day.
misconceptions.corrective: Without active rehearsal, short-term storage lasts only about 15 to 30 seconds and holds roughly 7 plus or minus 2 items — which is exactly why unwritten phone numbers vanish.

examples.text: Repeating a Wi-Fi password to yourself while crossing the room — stop rehearsing for half a minute and it is gone.

definition.text: Long-term memory (LTM) is the continuous storage of information, divided into explicit memories we consciously recall and implicit memories that operate outside consciousness.

anchor.quote: Long-term memory (LTM) is the continuous storage of information

facts.text: Unlike short-term memory, long-term storage capacity is believed to be unlimited.

anchor.quote: long-term memory storage capacity is believed to be unlimited

facts.text: Explicit memories are those we consciously try to remember, recall, and report.

anchor.quote: Explicit memories are those we consciously try to remember, recall, and report

facts.text: Implicit memories are long-term memories that are not part of our consciousness.

anchor.quote: Implicit memories are long-term memories that are not part of our consciousness

facts.text: Implicit procedural memory stores how to do things — the memory for skilled actions.

anchor.quote: Implicit procedural memory stores information about the way to do something, and it is the memory for skilled actions

facts.text: Explicit memory divides into episodic memory (events we have personally experienced) and semantic memory (knowledge about words, concepts, and facts).

anchor.quote: Episodic memory is information about events we have personally experienced

misconceptions.text: Students assume everything in long-term memory can be consciously recalled and described.
misconceptions.corrective: Implicit memories — including procedural memory for skilled actions — are long-term memories outside consciousness: you ride a bicycle reliably without being able to report the balance corrections you make.

examples.text: A pianist who cannot say which finger plays which note mid-piece, yet performs flawlessly — procedural memory running without conscious access.

definition.text: Forgetting arises at every stage of memory: encoding failure (the information never entered memory), storage decay over time, and retrieval failures such as blocking and interference.

anchor.quote: memory loss happens before the actual memory process begins, which is encoding failure

facts.text: We cannot remember something that was never stored in memory in the first place — encoding failure is not really forgetting.

anchor.quote: We can't remember something if we never stored it in our memory in the first place

facts.text: Ebbinghaus found storage decay is fast at first: an average person loses 50% of memorized information after 20 minutes and 70% after 24 hours, then the curve levels out.

anchor.quote: lose 50% of the memorized information after 20 minutes and 70% of the information after 24 hours

facts.text: Blocking is a retrieval failure where stored information is temporarily inaccessible — the tip-of-the-tongue state.

anchor.quote: you can't access stored information

facts.text: Proactive interference: old information hinders the recall of newly learned information.

anchor.quote: old information hinders the recall of newly learned information

facts.text: Retroactive interference: information learned more recently hinders the recall of older information.

anchor.quote: information learned more recently hinders the recall of older information

misconceptions.text: Students treat all forgetting as memories being erased from storage.
misconceptions.corrective: Much forgetting is encoding failure (never stored) or retrieval failure (blocking, interference) — the tip-of-the-tongue state proves information can remain stored yet be temporarily unreachable.

examples.text: Most people cannot draw a penny correctly despite seeing thousands — the details were never encoded, so there was nothing to forget.

definition.text: Piaget's theory holds that children do not think and reason like adults but move through four qualitatively different stages — sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational — building and revising schemata along the way.

anchor.quote: children do not think and reason like adults

facts.text: Children organize knowledge in schemata — concepts (mental models) used to categorize and interpret information — updating them by assimilation and accommodation.

anchor.quote: Schemata are concepts (mental models) that are used to help us categorize and interpret information

facts.text: In the sensorimotor stage (birth to about 2), the child develops object permanence — the understanding that something out of sight still exists.

anchor.quote: object permanence, which is the understanding that even if something is out of sight, it still exists

facts.text: In the preoperational stage (about 2 to 7), children display egocentrism and lack conservation — the idea that changing something's appearance does not change its amount.

anchor.quote: egocentrism, which means that the child is not able to take the perspective of others

facts.text: In the concrete operational stage (about 7 to 11), children can think logically about real, concrete events.

anchor.quote: In this stage, children can think logically about real (concrete) events

facts.text: In the formal operational stage (about age 11 to adulthood), thinkers can handle abstract ideas and hypothetical situations.

anchor.quote: children in the formal operational stage can also deal with abstract ideas and hypothetical situations

misconceptions.text: Students see children as miniature adults who simply know fewer facts.
misconceptions.corrective: Piaget showed the differences are qualitative: a preoperational child fails a conservation task not from missing information but because the required mental operations have not yet developed — telling them the answer does not fix it.

examples.text: Pour the same juice from a short wide cup into a tall thin glass: a four-year-old insists there is now more juice — conservation has not yet arrived.

mapping.stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational
mapping.dependency: each stage's mental operations are built from the schemata consolidated in the stage before
mapping.failure if skipped: instruction pitched above the child's stage produces imitation without understanding

definition.text: Erikson's psychosocial development theory emphasizes the social nature of development: across eight stages from infancy through late adulthood, each stage poses a conflict, or task, to resolve.

anchor.quote: psychosocial development theory emphasizes the social nature of our development

facts.text: Erikson proposed that personality development takes place all through the lifespan, not only in childhood.

anchor.quote: personality development takes place all through the lifespan

facts.text: We experience eight stages of development over our lifespan, from infancy through late adulthood.

anchor.quote: we experience eight stages of development over our lifespan, from infancy through late adulthood

facts.text: At each stage there is a conflict, or task, that we need to resolve.

anchor.quote: At each stage there is a conflict, or task, that we need to resolve

facts.text: Infancy's task (birth to 12 months) is trust versus mistrust, with trust as the basis of development.

anchor.quote: trust is the basis of our development during infancy

facts.text: Adolescents (ages 12–18) face identity versus role confusion; the main task is developing a sense of self.

anchor.quote: children face the task of identity versus role confusion

misconceptions.text: Students assume personality development is finished by the end of childhood.
misconceptions.corrective: Erikson's eight psychosocial stages run from infancy through late adulthood — adults still face new conflicts such as intimacy, generativity, and integrity; development is lifelong.

examples.text: A college first-year cycling through majors, friend groups, and aesthetics is doing the normal work of identity versus role confusion — exploration, not flakiness.

definition.text: Theories of intelligence disagree on its structure: Spearman saw one general factor (g) that can be measured and compared, while Sternberg's triarchic theory and Gardner's multiple intelligences carve it into several distinct capacities.

anchor.quote: intelligence consisted of one general factor, called g, which could be measured and compared among individuals

facts.text: Spearman proposed a single general factor, g, measurable and comparable across individuals.

anchor.quote: Charles Spearman believed intelligence consisted of one general factor, called g

facts.text: Crystallized intelligence is acquired knowledge and the ability to retrieve it.

anchor.quote: Crystallized intelligence is characterized as acquired knowledge and the ability to retrieve it

facts.text: Fluid intelligence is the ability to see complex relationships and solve problems.

anchor.quote: Fluid intelligence encompasses the ability to see complex relationships and solve problems

facts.text: Sternberg's triarchic theory splits intelligence into practical ('street smarts'), analytical (academic problem solving), and creative (inventing solutions) parts.

anchor.quote: the triarchic theory of intelligence because it sees intelligence as comprised of three parts

facts.text: In Gardner's theory, each person possesses at least eight intelligences.

anchor.quote: In Gardner's theory, each person possesses at least eight intelligences

misconceptions.text: Students treat an IQ score as identical to intelligence itself.
misconceptions.corrective: A test score is one operationalization of the construct: it captures Spearman's comparable general factor, but Sternberg's practical and creative intelligences and Gardner's eight-plus intelligences fall largely outside a single number.

examples.text: A top mechanic who never finished school diagnoses engine faults instantly (practical intelligence) yet scores unremarkably on a paper IQ test — the measure misses the capacity.

definition.text: Motivation describes the wants or needs that direct behavior toward a goal; intrinsically motivated behaviors are performed for the personal satisfaction they bring, while extrinsically motivated behaviors are performed to receive something from others.

anchor.quote: Motivation describes the wants or needs that direct behavior toward a goal

facts.text: Intrinsic motivation comes from the sense of personal satisfaction a behavior brings; extrinsic motivation aims to receive something from others.

anchor.quote: Intrinsically motivated behaviors are performed because of the sense of personal satisfaction that they bring

facts.text: Being paid for an activity we already enjoy can lead the behavior to be thought of as work that no longer provides the same enjoyment.

anchor.quote: leads to those behaviors being thought of as work no longer providing that same enjoyment

facts.text: The overjustification effect: intrinsic motivation is diminished when extrinsic motivation is given.

anchor.quote: the overjustification effect—intrinsic motivation is diminished when extrinsic motivation is given

facts.text: Real motivation is usually a mix of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and the mix can change over time.

anchor.quote: our motivations are often a mix of both intrinsic and extrinsic factors

misconceptions.text: Students (and teachers) assume adding rewards always strengthens motivation.
misconceptions.corrective: The overjustification effect shows the opposite can happen: paying or prizing an activity someone already enjoys can recast it as work and diminish the intrinsic motivation that was driving it.

examples.text: A reading-for-pizza program gets reluctant readers started (extrinsic), but a child who already devours novels may read less once reading becomes a transaction.

definition.text: A problem-solving strategy is a plan of action used to find a solution; the main families are algorithms (exact step-by-step formulas) and heuristics (general frameworks that trade certainty for speed).

anchor.quote: A problem-solving strategy is a plan of action used to find a solution

facts.text: An algorithm is a problem-solving formula providing step-by-step instructions to achieve a desired outcome.

anchor.quote: An algorithm is a problem-solving formula that provides you with step-by-step instructions used to achieve a desired outcome

facts.text: A heuristic is a general problem-solving framework rather than an exact recipe.

anchor.quote: A heuristic is a general problem-solving framework

facts.text: People reach for heuristics under specific conditions — for example, when faced with too much information or when decision time is limited.

anchor.quote: When one is faced with too much information; When the time to make a decision is limited

facts.text: A mental set is persisting with an approach that worked in the past but is clearly not working now.

anchor.quote: you persist in approaching a problem in a way that has worked in the past but is clearly not working now

facts.text: Functional fixedness is a mental set in which you cannot perceive an object being used for anything other than its designed purpose.

anchor.quote: you cannot perceive an object being used for something other than what it was designed for

misconceptions.text: Students dismiss heuristics as sloppy thinking that should always be replaced by algorithms.
misconceptions.corrective: Heuristics are adaptive general frameworks deliberately used when information or time is limited; an algorithm guarantees a result only where a step-by-step formula exists and there is time to run it.

examples.text: Working backwards from a paper's due date to set draft and research milestones — a heuristic the textbook itself recommends for planning.
